title: The Loyalty Lift

scenario.situation: Loyalty-program members spend an average of $1,840 per year versus $610 for non-members — a 3× gap that has leadership excited.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The VP of Growth believes the loyalty program itself drives higher spend and wants to auto-enroll all customers to replicate the effect.
scenario.question: Does the loyalty program actually cause members to spend more, or is something else driving the gap?

decisions.prompt: Leadership wants a rollout plan. How do you frame your investigation before committing to that recommendation?

options.label: Quantify the revenue upside of full enrollment
options.detail: Project how much total spend would increase if the non-member base spent at the member rate.
options.consequence: You produce a compelling $42M upside slide — but you've accepted the causal premise without testing it. If the program didn't create the spend gap, the projection is fiction.
options.divergenceCost: Accepted leadership's causal premise and modeled a number that may be entirely illusory.

options.label: Compare members and age-matched non-members
options.detail: Ask whether the spend gap persists when you control for how long customers have been active — isolate tenure and enrollment timing.
options.consequence: You notice that members had to accumulate purchase history just to qualify for enrollment. Matching non-members by account age and prior activity reveals the gap nearly disappears — the program selected already-active buyers.

options.label: Survey members on what drives their loyalty
options.detail: Ask members directly whether the program changed their shopping behavior.
options.consequence: Members report loving the program — but self-reported attribution is heavily biased toward recency and salience. You learn nothing about counterfactual behavior.
options.divergenceCost: Relied on self-reported attribution, which can't reveal what customers would have spent without the program.

options.label: Build a propensity model to predict who will benefit most
options.detail: Model likelihood of spend lift from enrollment and target the highest-propensity customers.
options.consequence: The model is well-specified but trained on data contaminated by the same bias — it will predict high lift for customers who are already highly active, reinforcing the illusion.
options.divergenceCost: Modeled on biased data, encoding the confound into every future targeting decision.

decisions.prompt: You decide to compare groups more carefully. Which metric do you use to assess whether the program lifts spend?

artifact.title: Average annual spend — members vs. non-members (raw)
artifact.caption: Raw average spend. Members appear to spend 3× more — but members must shop for 90 days before enrolling. That pre-enrollment window is not counted against non-members.

options.label: Raw average annual spend: all members vs. all non-members
options.detail: Compare the mean full-year spend for each group as-is.
options.consequence: The 3× gap looks airtight — but members had to survive 90 days of active shopping just to enroll. Non-members include brand-new and lapsed customers. You're comparing apples to fruit salad.
options.divergenceCost: Included the immortal pre-enrollment period in the member average while mixing all-tenure non-members into the baseline.

options.label: Post-enrollment spend vs. spend of tenure-matched non-members
options.detail: Measure only spend after enrollment date for members, and match non-members who have been active for the same duration.
options.consequence: Once you exclude the pre-enrollment period and match on account age, the gap collapses from 3× to 1.07×. Members and active non-members of the same tenure spend almost identically — the program is selecting high spenders, not creating them.

artifact.title: Spend AFTER enrollment date vs. tenure-matched non-members
artifact.caption: Controlling for the immortal pre-enrollment window and matching tenure, the spend gap shrinks to 7% — far below the raw 200% gap. The program is selecting active buyers, not activating passive ones.

decisions.prompt: Post-enrollment, tenure-matched spend is nearly identical between members and non-members. What do you tell the VP of Growth?

options.label: "The loyalty program has no effect — cancel it."
options.detail: Conclude the program is worthless and recommend discontinuing it.
options.consequence: You've overcorrected. The corrected analysis shows no detectable lift — but it doesn't prove zero effect. The program may still drive retention or basket mix in ways this metric misses, and killing it without a proper test risks real harm.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a null causal result from observational data and skipped a controlled test.

options.label: "The raw gap is driven by selection, not the program — let's run a randomized enrollment test before any rollout."
options.detail: Present the immortal-time finding, explain the bias, and recommend a holdout experiment to measure true lift.
options.consequence: You've reframed the narrative with evidence: the 3× figure reflects who joins the program, not what it does to them. Leadership understands why auto-enrollment won't replicate the gap, and a randomized test is greenlit to find the real effect size.

insight: The 3× spend gap existed because customers had to shop actively for 90 days before qualifying to enroll — that pre-enrollment period guaranteed members were already high-value buyers, and it was invisible in the raw comparison. This is immortal time bias: the outcome (low spend) literally could not be observed during the qualification window, inflating the treated group's average. The lesson is that whenever group membership requires surviving a qualifying period, any metric spanning that period is contaminated — the fix is to measure only post-enrollment outcomes and match controls on the same tenure baseline.
